summary: The study has a commendable paired design: identical pilots for all methods, group-disjoint splits, deterministic seeds, released per-pilot outputs, a pre-registration and a time-stamped log. The headline result that RPM is more accurate than inverse-power-law extrapolation (IPL3) is robust: I reproduced it at the source level, where RPM is better in 9/9 sources. However, the experimental design does not support the paper's more nuanced conclusions about FLAT, SLOPE-T, RPM-w, calibrated bands and sample-size decisions. (1) The ground truth (log of the mean MSE of LOGO-tuned ridge over random draws) is a different estimand from what RPM forecasts (oracle-tuned theory) and from the pilot anchor (selection-optimistic min-CV). The pilot CV lies 0.19/0.11/0.06 log units below the truth at n0=50/100/200, and the LOGO-tuning excess is 0.03–0.08. Both offsets exceed the 0.01–0.03 differences between the leading methods, and re-scoring against the oracle-tuned truth reorders them. (2) The 38 tasks come from about 9 independent sample collections. At the source level, RPM-w is not better than RPM (5/9, p=0.65). (3) Pooling unbalanced horizon cells hides the fact that RPM is significantly worse than FLAT on a balanced cell set (9/38, p=0.006) and in every stratum. (4) The decision and gain metrics splice unanchored RPM curves onto the pilot CV and are dominated by pilot noise and grid truncation; the reported decision endpoint deviates from the pre-registered one. (5) The curve baselines and IPL3 bands are distorted by a 1e-12 numerical floor. (6) Post-hoc elements (SLOPE-T, conformal bands, RPM-w) appear unlabelled in the Abstract and Significance; the timing statements conflict with the logs, and code was changed during the main run. The conformal bands reach nominal coverage only marginally: coverage is 29–50% for CGL, Tablets and Diesel at nominal 80%. The PLS-truth analysis is not a PLS forecasting test. The SLOPE-T slope mixes n-ranges.
strengths: All forecasters are evaluated on identical, deterministically seeded pilots with group-disjoint test sets and LOGO cross-validation inside pilots. Leakage control is careful: unlabelled spectra come from the pool only, and replicates are averaged before splitting.

A pre-registration, a time-stamped decision log and the ICRAF-VisNIR sensitivity analysis are provided. Negative results are reported (RPM-T failure, poor decision metric, under-covering bootstrap bands).
Per-pilot raw forecasts and full ground-truth arrays, including test MSE at every penalty, are released. This made independent re-analysis possible and is exemplary.
The RPM-vs-IPL3 advantage survives every re-analysis I ran: source-level (9/9 sources), balanced horizon cells (27/38) and oracle-tuned truth (33/38).

issues.title: Ground-truth estimand does not match what the forecasters estimate; the resulting offsets are larger than the method differences the conclusions rest on
issues.description: The reference is log sqrt of the MEAN test MSE over 30/16/8 random calibration sets of LOGO-tuned ridge (learning_curves.truth_curve). The forecasters estimate other quantities. RPM forecasts the ORACLE-tuned theory risk min_mu E(n,mu) (theory.optimal_risk). FLAT, SLOPE-T and the decision curves are anchored on the pilot's min-over-53-penalties LOGO error, which is a selection-optimistic estimate. None of these three quantities equals the reference, and the gaps depend on n, so they distort both level and slope. The pilot CV error lies well below the truth at the same n0. FLAT is accurate partly because this anchor optimism cancels the improvement FLAT leaves out. This is a compensating bias of the kind the authors themselves dismiss for the mango season shift ('compensating biases, not skill'). Changing the estimand to the oracle-tuned truth, which is what RPM's equation targets, reorders the leading methods. So the headline statements 'the pilot's own CV error and SLOPE-T were equally accurate' and 'RPM vs FLAT n.s.' are not robust to the definition of the truth. The theory-validity figures (0.113/0.126, Section 4.1) also compare an oracle-tuned curve with LOGO-tuned truth, so they mix theory misfit with tuning excess.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw/truth_*.npz: the LOGO-tuning excess, 0.5*log(ridge_mse / min_mu ridge_mu_mse), is median 0.075 at n=50 (max 0.52), 0.042 at n=100, 0.030 at n=200 and 0.006 at n=6400. From raw_results.csv, the pilot CV log-RMSE minus the LOGO-tuned truth at n=n0 is mean -0.187 (median -0.150) at n0=50, -0.107 at n0=100 and -0.055 at n0=200; against the oracle truth it is -0.081, -0.032 and -0.022. The across-repetition CV of MSE at n=50 is median 0.39 (max 1.11), which implies a Jensen gap between log(mean MSE) and the typical calibration of about 0.035 log units at the median under a lognormal approximation. Re-scoring all 10,700 forecasts per method against the oracle-tuned truth (min over mu of ridge_mu_mse) gives mean task errors of SLOPE-T 0.228, RPM-w 0.262, FLAT 0.269 and RPM 0.275. SLOPE-T then beats FLAT on 29/38 tasks (raw Wilcoxon p=0.0007; the paper has p=0.16), and RPM vs FLAT p=0.60. Compare Table 2: SLOPE-T 0.251, FLAT 0.266, RPM 0.284.
issues.corrective_action: State the estimand explicitly: the expected MSE over calibration draws, or the RMSE of the user's single realised calibration. Make each forecaster target that estimand. Either add the CV-tuning excess to RPM's forecast or score RPM against the oracle-tuned truth, and report both truths in Table 2. Report the anchor bias (pilot CV vs truth at n0) as a result in its own right. Decompose every method's error into an anchor (level) component and a gain (slope) component, and qualify the FLAT and SLOPE-T conclusions accordingly. Repeat the Section 4.1 validity numbers against an oracle-tuned truth.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the ground-truth stage storing the per-repetition test MSE, at the selected penalty and at every penalty, so that (i) the median and mean log RMSE over calibration draws and (ii) the oracle-tuned curve are available. Re-score all existing forecasts against each definition. This is cheap: about 30 min for all 38 tasks according to run_full.log.

issues.title: Pseudo-replication: 38 'tasks' are not independent units; source-level re-analysis changes several significance claims
issues.description: Section 3.7 uses the task as the unit for Wilcoxon tests with n=38. The tasks come from 9 sample collections and share spectra within a library: 4 properties per OSSL library, 6 diesel properties on the same spectra, 4 CGL and 3 Tecator properties. In addition, ICRAF-MIR and ICRAF-VisNIR are the same 4,153 soil samples, and KSSL-MIR and KSSL-VisNIR share 20,969 layer IDs. Errors within a library are strongly correlated because they share spectra, pilots drawn from similar pools, and test sets. The effective sample size is therefore about 9 sources, not 38. The claims of a significant RPM-w advantage over RPM (Holm p=0.023) and of SLOPE-T over RPM rest on within-library replication.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from raw_results.csv (per-task mean |log err|, then averaged within source; source definition as in analysis.source_of). RPM vs IPL3: RPM better in 9/9 sources (Wilcoxon p=0.004), so this claim is robust. RPM vs RPM-w: RPM-w better in only 5/9 sources (p=0.65); RPM-w is worse than RPM for Mango (0.300 vs 0.243), CGL, Tablets and Tecator. RPM vs FLAT: FLAT better in 7/9 sources (p=0.13). RPM vs SLOPE-T: SLOPE-T better in 7/9 (p=0.039). Sample-ID overlap was checked in code/data/cache/ossl_*.npz: ICRAF mir/visnir 4153/4153 shared; KSSL mir/visnir 20,969 shared.
issues.corrective_action: Use a hierarchical analysis: a mixed model with source and library random effects, or a cluster bootstrap and permutation by source. Report source-level paired tests alongside the task-level ones. Remove or qualify the claim that RPM-w significantly improves on RPM, including recommendation (vi), which promotes RPM-w.

issues.title: Unbalanced pilot-size and horizon mix per task makes the pooled primary endpoint an incomparable average; under a balanced design the pre-registered RPM is significantly worse than FLAT
issues.description: The primary endpoint averages over all available (n0, n) cells within each task. The number of cells varies widely: 60 to 520 forecast rows per task. Tecator and CGL contribute only ratios 2–4 with n0 ≤ 50, KSSL contributes ratios up to 256, and n0=200 exists for only 25 tasks. Per-task means therefore average different mixtures of easy and hard cells, and the pooled 'RPM vs FLAT not significant' result depends on this mixture. In both a balanced short-extrapolation subset and the long-extrapolation stratum, RPM is less accurate than FLAT.
issues.evidence: Recomputed on the cells available for all 38 tasks (n0=25 with ratios 2 and 4, n0=50 with ratio 2): FLAT 0.255, SLOPE-T 0.263, RPM-w 0.294, RPM 0.301, IPL3 0.348. RPM is better than FLAT on only 9/38 tasks (Wilcoxon p=0.006) and better than SLOPE-T on 12/38 (p=0.002). Table S10, ratio ≥16: RPM 0.317 vs FLAT 0.284 vs SLOPE-T 0.263. Table S7: FLAT ≤ RPM at every n0 (0.329/0.373, 0.236/0.247, 0.200/0.229, 0.139/0.164).
issues.corrective_action: Define the primary comparison on a balanced grid of (n0, n/n0) cells, or fit a mixed model with fixed cell effects and task and source random effects. Report cell-wise results in the main text. Rephrase Section 4.3 so that it does not imply parity between RPM and FLAT when RPM is worse in every stratum.

issues.title: Decision metric and post-hoc gain analysis are structurally biased: the RPM curve is not anchored consistently, many outcomes are fixed by pilot noise or grid truncation, and the reported endpoint differs from the pre-registered one
issues.description: The pre-registration (E5) specifies the error |log2(n_hat/n*)| with failures. The manuscript reports the share 'within a factor of two' and constructs each curve by prepending the pilot CV value at n0 to the method's unanchored forecasts (analysis.decision_table). Anchoring is not in the pre-registration. RPM's forecasts are not anchored on the pilot CV, so its spliced curve is frequently non-monotone. For a large share of pilots every method returns n_hat=n0, so the outcome is decided by pilot noise rather than by the method. Where n* equals the largest truth size, a forecast that reaches the target just beyond n* is scored as 'never reaches', which structurally penalises conservative methods. FLAT cannot succeed by construction. The post-hoc gain error (Table S22/S23) computes RPM's predicted gain as fc(n) minus the pilot CV rather than relative to RPM's own level at n0. This inflates RPM's gain bias (+0.209) and confounds level with slope.
issues.evidence: From raw_results.csv: RPM's forecast at n=2n0 exceeds the pilot CV in 39.5% of pilots (RPM-w 41.7%; mean difference -0.035). This explains RPM's 51.4%/66.4% 'never reaches target' rates (Table S21). The pilot CV is already ≤ the target T=truth(n*) in 31.7% (n*=4n0) and 12.8% (n*=16n0) of pilots, which forces n_hat=n0 (error = 2 or 4 doublings) for every method. n* equals the largest truth size in 17.8% (4n0) and 23.0% (16n0) of cases. FLAT: 0% success by construction (Table S21).
issues.corrective_action: Report the pre-registered endpoint (|log2 error|, with failures treated as right-censored or assigned the grid maximum) as primary. Build every method's curve from its own forecast at n0, or anchor all methods identically by multiplicative rescaling. Restrict n* to at most half the largest truth size. Recompute the gain error relative to each method's own n0 forecast. Consider a loss-based decision metric, such as the expected cost of over- or under-collecting samples, which does not exclude FLAT by construction.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the forecasters on the existing pilots with n0 added to the horizon list, so that each method's own level at n0 is stored. The per-pilot cost is about 1.5 s (Table S31). Then recompute Table S21–S23 and Fig. S1.

issues.title: Curve-fitting baselines and their uncertainty bands are implemented in a way that produces numerical-floor artefacts, so the reported baseline errors and coverage are not intrinsic properties of the methods
issues.description: The IPL/EXP/LOG curves are fitted to MSE, not log RMSE, with weights sigma=1/sqrt(m). Forecasts are clipped at MSE=1e-12. LOG2 is clipped inside the model. DF-OLS collapses to about 0 when the pilot ridge nearly interpolates (s2 = RSS/max(n0-df-1,1)). The IPL3 delta-method bands are symmetric on the MSE scale and their lower limits are clipped at 1e-12. As a result, the LOG2, EXP3 and DF-OLS mean errors in Table 2 and the abstract are dominated by the arbitrary floor. IPL3's 83% coverage and its 'absurd' width factor of 7.8×10^5 (Section 4.5, Table S19) are produced by clipping, not by the method. A practitioner would fit learning curves in log space and use log-scale or bootstrap intervals, so the comparison of band quality between RPM and IPL3 is not fair. The headline RPM-vs-IPL3 accuracy result is not affected: IPL3 point forecasts never hit the floor.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from raw_results.csv: 70.8% of LOG2 forecasts sit at the 1e-12 floor; LOG2 mean |log err| excluding floored rows is 0.488 vs 9.83 over all rows (Table 2 task mean 10.127). EXP3 is 6.9% floored (1.69 excluding floored rows). DF-OLS is 4.0% floored (0.425 excluding vs 1.106 over all rows; Table 2 1.272). IPL3: 69.7% of lower 80% limits and 76.8% of lower 95% limits sit at the floor. Code: forecasters.CURVES, curve_forecast (np.maximum(..., 1e-12)), dfols_forecast.
issues.corrective_action: Refit the curve baselines in log-RMSE space with a positive asymptote, for example bounded below by a fraction of the pilot CV. Compute bands on the log scale or by bootstrap of the within-pilot curve. Report fit failures and floor hits as a separate failure rate instead of averaging enormous log errors. Correct the claims about DF-OLS, EXP3, LOG2 and IPL3 bands in Section 4.3/4.5 and the abstract. Cite a source for the DF-OLS formula or drop it.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the IPL3/IPL2/EXP3/LOG2/DF-OLS baselines on the identical pilots with log-space fitting and log-scale/bootstrap bands. This costs about 0.5 s per pilot (Table S31).

issues.title: Post-hoc additions are not reported transparently enough relative to the pre-registered method; the timeline in the manuscript conflicts with the logs, and code changed during the main run
issues.description: (i) The Abstract and Significance present SLOPE-T (0.251) and the leave-one-source-out (LOSO) calibrated bands as findings and planning recommendations without marking them as post hoc. SLOPE-T was defined (EXPERIMENT_LOG 14:53) after the partial inspection showing FLAT beating RPM (19:41) and after RPM-T was seen to fail (14:50). (ii) Recommendation (vi) promotes RPM-w, a post-hoc variant whose advantage over RPM is fragile: Table S15 gives Holm p=0.107 excluding ICRAF-VisNIR, and the source-level comparison gives 5/9. (iii) Section 3.6 says RPM-w 'was specified after the main run had been executed'. The log and results/experiment_logs/run_full.log show it was implemented at 19:24–19:27, while the main run (19:20:20–19:47:01) was still executing. (iv) At 19:45, during the same run, the fit_rpm optimiser start value was changed for tasks processed by 're-spawned workers', so the main arm may mix code versions. In the current code the changed start value lt0 = log(.../sum(ln**r0)) is also used for the fixed-r (r0=r_fix=1) fits, which contradicts the log's statement that only RPM-rfree is affected. (v) The 'Main stage complete' log row is dated 2026-11-16 14:40, although the run log shows the main stage ended at 19:47 the previous day. (vi) The Holm family was enlarged from the 6 pre-registered baselines to 10 comparisons that include post-hoc variants. As a result, SLOPE-T vs RPM appears with Holm p=0.031 (Table 2/S8) and p=0.046 (Table S9). (vii) The manuscript text refers to a 'hostile-reviewer check' (Section 3.6, line 123), which is internal process language.
issues.evidence: EXPERIMENT_LOG.md rows 19:24–19:27, 19:41, 19:45 (both), 14:40, 14:50 and 14:53. results/experiment_logs/run_full.log start/end stamps. code/src/models/forecasters.py fit_rpm (lt0 uses r0=r_fix for fixed modes). manuscript_full.md lines 13, 15, 121, 123 and 269. Tables S8, S9 and S15.
issues.corrective_action: Label every post-hoc element as such in the Abstract, Significance and Conclusions. Restrict confirmatory statements to the pre-registered RPM vs the pre-registered baselines, using the pre-registered Holm family. Correct the RPM-w timing statement and the log entries. Re-run the main stage from scratch with the frozen final code and report that RPM and baseline outputs are identical, or report the differences, together with a code hash. Remove the internal 'hostile-reviewer' wording. Present SLOPE-T and the calibrated bands as hypotheses that require external validation.
issues.proposed_experiment: (a) A clean re-run of 'run_all.py --stage main' with the final code and a byte-level comparison of forecasts_main_*.csv (about 27 min). (b) External validation of SLOPE-T and the conformal bands on calibration data sets not used anywhere in this study, including in slope estimation.

issues.title: LOSO split-conformal bands reach nominal coverage only marginally (pooled over rows dominated by large soil tasks); coverage conditional on source is far below nominal for the small non-soil sets
issues.description: Section 4.5 and the Abstract claim that the calibrated bands 'reached nominal coverage' and that 'honest 80% bands span a factor of 1.77–2.05'. Coverage is pooled over forecast rows, and KSSL/ICRAF tasks contribute up to 520 rows each. For the small and non-soil sources the bands severely under-cover. In addition, the bands are scored against the expected RMSE over calibration draws, not against the RMSE of the single calibration a user will actually build (see R3-C01-01). The realised RMSE varies further (CV of MSE across draws median 0.39 at n=50), so the bands understate planning uncertainty. A nested-LOSO correction is not needed: I recomputed SLOPE-T bands with the target source excluded from the other sources' slope priors, and coverage changed from 79.3% to 79.4%.
issues.evidence: Recomputed with the authors' procedure (analysis.run_analysis, T16 block). SLOPE-T at nominal 80%: coverage by source CGL 29%, Tablets 38%, Diesel 50%, Tecator 76%, AfSIS1 81%, KSSL 81%, ICRAF 88%; task-mean 71.0% (rows 79.3%). At nominal 95%: CGL 58%, Diesel 72%; task-mean 88.7%. RPM-w at 80%: Tablets 33%, Diesel 55%, CGL 57%, Mango 66%; task-mean 74.3%.
issues.corrective_action: Report task-mean and source-conditional coverage. Use Mondrian (group-conditional) conformal calibration by data-set family or pool size, or widen bands for small and designed data sets. Calibrate and score bands against the realised RMSE of single calibrations, which requires per-repetition truth (R3-C01-01). Revise the statements in the Abstract, 4.5 and 4.10(iii).
issues.proposed_experiment: Use the per-repetition truth from R3-C01-01 to score the bands as prediction intervals for a single future calibration.

issues.title: The 'PLS ground truth' analysis is not a test of forecasting PLS learning curves, and the claim that the ordering was unchanged is incorrect
issues.description: All forecasters are built on ridge fitted to the pilot: the anchor is the ridge pilot CV and the IPL curves use ridge within-pilot. They are then scored against PLS truth. PLS truth is systematically higher than ridge truth, so this analysis mostly measures the ridge–PLS gap and mechanically favours pessimistic forecasts. It does not show that a PLS user, who would have a PLS pilot CV error, could forecast a PLS curve. The ordering did change: FLAT is the most accurate method against the PLS truth.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from truth_*.npz: 0.5*log(pls_mse/ridge_mse) has a mean of +0.039 over tasks, is positive in 37/38 tasks and ranges up to 0.19. Table S12 (PLS truth): FLAT 0.253 < SLOPE-T 0.263 < RPM-w 0.266 < RPM 0.279. Table S6 (ridge truth): SLOPE-T 0.251 < FLAT 0.266 < RPM-w 0.271 < RPM 0.284. Table S13: RPM vs FLAT raw p=0.027 (Holm 0.055) against PLS truth. Manuscript line 198: 'Against the PLS ground truth the ordering was unchanged'.
issues.corrective_action: Either run a genuine PLS forecasting arm (PLS pilot CV anchor for FLAT and SLOPE-T, PLS within-pilot curves for IPL3, and RPM mapped to PLS), or retitle the analysis 'ridge-based forecasts scored against PLS truth'. Correct the 'ordering unchanged' statement.
issues.proposed_experiment: PLS forecasting arm on the identical pilots: grouped-CV PLS pilot error and PLS sub-sampling curves for FLAT, SLOPE-T and IPL3.

issues.title: The transferred slope (SLOPE-T and the '8.3% per doubling' rule) mixes n-ranges; because learning curves are concave in log-log, the slope depends on the range over which it is measured
issues.description: Each task's slope is a single linear fit of log RMSE on log2 n over that task's own truth grid (analysis.add_slope_transfer): 50–100 for CGL and Tecator, 50–200 for Diesel, 50–6400 for KSSL. The LOSO median used by SLOPE-T and the recommended 8.3% per doubling therefore pool slopes from different regimes. The curves flatten with n, so the rule is too steep for long or large-n extrapolations and too shallow for short, small-n ones. This also feeds the 'slopes are remarkably similar' argument in Section 4.2.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from truth_*.npz, for tasks with max n ≥ 800 (24 tasks): median slope -0.101 over n=50–400, -0.048 over n ≥ 400, -0.081 over the full range. Median full-range slope by maximum truth size: max n=100 → -0.254, 200 → -0.121, 400 → -0.059, 800 → -0.086, 1600 → -0.067, 6400 → -0.081.
issues.corrective_action: Estimate slopes on a common n-range, or model slope as a function of n (or n/p), and transfer the slope matched to the pilot's n0..n range. Report how sensitive SLOPE-T is to the slope definition (median vs mean; full vs matched range). Replace the single 8.3% figure in the Abstract and recommendation (ii) with a range-specific statement.

issues.title: Dataset design: small, designed and single-split tasks give noisy and partly non-random ground truth, and soil libraries dominate
issues.description: 13 of 38 tasks (Diesel 6, Tecator 3, CGL 4) have pools of 173–296 and group-disjoint test sets of 58–99 samples, with one fixed test split per task. For Tecator and CGL, truth calibrations of n=100 are drawn from a pool of 173–180, so repetitions overlap heavily with each other and with the 50-sample pilots. With 58–60 test samples, the test-set sampling SE of log RMSE is about 0.09 (≈0.5·sqrt(2/58) for Gaussian residuals). This is comparable to the 0.01–0.05 differences between methods and is shared across horizons, which favours methods whose bias happens to offset it. The CGL mixtures come from a designed experiment, which violates the random-sampling premise that the paper itself states. Meanwhile 23/38 tasks are soils, and the non-soil sets allow only ratios 2–8, so the long-extrapolation conclusions rest almost entirely on 3–4 soil collections.
issues.evidence: Table S1: n test 58–99 for CGL, Tecator and Diesel; pools 173–296; max n truth 100–200. Table S7: n0=100/200 available for only 31/25 tasks. Table S10: the ratio ≥16 stratum has 25 tasks, all soil or mango (Table 1 max n). Limitations item 5 acknowledges a single test split.
issues.corrective_action: Use repeated group-disjoint test splits (for example 5) and propagate the test-split variance into the task-level errors. Analyse designed and small sets separately from random-sample populations. Add large non-soil data sets (food, feed, pharmaceutical or agricultural, with more than 1,000 samples each) so that long extrapolations are not soil-only.
issues.proposed_experiment: Repeated-split ground truth for the small sets, and the addition of at least two large non-soil calibration data sets.

issues.title: Reporting inconsistencies
issues.description: Several cross-references and statistics are inconsistent. They do not change conclusions but undermine traceability.
issues.evidence: (a) Section 4.7 cites 'Supplementary Tables S21–S22' for the simulation, but the simulation tables are S26–S27; S21–S22 are decision and gain tables. (b) SLOPE-T vs RPM Holm p is 0.031 (Table 2, S8) and 0.046 (Table S9) because the families differ; this is not explained. (c) The Table S10 caption says 'short: < 16' but the stratum is labelled 'ratio <= 8'. (d) The Table 2 caption lists RPM-w/RPM-T/RPM-wT/SLOPE-T as post hoc, but the '117,700 forecasts' total in Section 4.3 counts post-hoc methods, while the abstract's '2,640 pilots' framing implies a single pre-registered evaluation.
issues.corrective_action: Fix the cross-references, state the Holm family for every p-value, and harmonise the captions.

recommendation_rationale: The core empirical contribution (theory-based forecasts are far less optimistic than power-law extrapolation) is sound and reproducible. The paper's practical conclusions, however, depend on design choices that are not justified or not robust. These conclusions are: that FLAT and SLOPE-T are 'equally accurate' to or better than RPM, that RPM-w improves on RPM, that calibrated bands reach nominal coverage, and that sample sizes cannot be forecast. The design choices are the ground-truth estimand, the pilot anchoring, task-level pseudo-replication, horizon weighting, decision-metric construction and baseline floors. Most fixes are re-analyses of the released outputs. A few cheap re-runs are needed: per-repetition truth, n0-level forecasts, log-space curve baselines, a clean main-stage re-run and a PLS arm. External validation of the post-hoc SLOPE-T rule is needed before it is recommended in the Abstract. None of this requires abandoning the study, so major revision rather than rejection is appropriate.
